lessons.title: Real vs. personal property, fixtures, and legal descriptions
lessons.body:
## What "real property" means

Everything a broker sells falls into one of two buckets: real property or personal property. The exam tests the line between them constantly, because the line decides what transfers with a deed and what has to be handled with a bill of sale.

- **[[Land]]** is the earth's surface, everything below it to the center of the earth, and the airspace above it, plus things permanently attached by nature (trees, minerals in place).
- **[[Real estate]]** is land plus everything people permanently attach to it (buildings, fences, paving).
- **[[Real property]]** is real estate plus the legal rights that come with owning it. These rights are often described as the [[bundle of rights]]: possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, and disposition.

**[[Personal property]]** (also called *personalty* or *chattels*) is everything movable that isn't real property: furniture, cars, a refrigerator that just plugs in. Personal property transfers by a **[[bill of sale]]**, not a deed.

### Rights that can be separated

Ownership can be split into layers, and each layer can be sold or leased separately:

| Right | Covers | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Surface rights | The land's surface | Selling a lot but keeping minerals |
| Subsurface (mineral) rights | Oil, gas, minerals below | An oil company leases mineral rights |
| Air rights | Space above the surface | Selling air rights over a rail yard for a building platform |

Rights and privileges that "run with" the land, such as an easement benefiting the lot or water rights tied to it, are called [[appurtenances]]. They transfer automatically with the property unless the deed says otherwise.

### Water rights in brief

Many eastern states follow **[[Riparian rights|riparian]]** rights (owners along a river share reasonable use) and **[[Littoral rights|littoral]]** rights (owners along a lake or ocean). Many western states, including Colorado, use **[[prior appropriation]]**: the first person to put water to beneficial use has the senior right, regardless of who owns the riverbank. Colorado water rights are covered in the state portion of this course.

## Crops: emblements vs. natural growth

- **[[Fructus naturales]]** (trees, perennial shrubs, grass) grow without yearly planting. They're treated as real property.
- **[[Fructus industriales]]** are annual crops planted by human labor (wheat, corn). They're personal property, and they're called [[emblements]]. A tenant farmer who planted a crop generally has the right to come back and harvest it even if the lease ends before harvest, provided the tenant didn't cause the lease to end.

## Fixtures

A **[[fixture]]** is an item that was personal property but has been attached to real property in a way that makes it part of the real estate. A ceiling fan in the box is personal property; once it's wired into the ceiling, it's a fixture and transfers with the house unless the contract excludes it.

Courts use a handful of tests, often remembered as **MARIA**:

- **M**ethod of attachment: is it bolted, nailed, plumbed or wired in? Would removal damage the property?
- **A**daptability: was the item customized for this property (custom-cut blinds, a built-in bookcase)?
- **R**elationship of the parties: courts favor buyers over sellers, and tenants over landlords.
- **I**ntention: did the person who attached it intend it to be permanent? Courts treat intention as the most important test.
- **A**greement: a written agreement between the parties overrides the other tests.

> **Heads-up on "most important":** Courts treat the intention of the person who attached the item as the controlling test, judged objectively from how it was attached and adapted. Some prep courses, including Van Ed's quizzes, instead key **[[method of attachment]]** as the most important test. Answer each source on its own terms; on any exam, a written agreement between the parties beats every other test.

> **Exam tip:** The easiest way to prevent a fixture dispute is to address it in the purchase contract. If the seller wants to keep the dining-room chandelier, list it as excluded, or swap it out before showing the home.

### Trade fixtures

A **[[trade fixture]]** is equipment a tenant installs for a business: restaurant ovens, store shelving, a salon's chairs. Trade fixtures stay the tenant's personal property. The tenant must remove them by the end of the lease and repair any damage caused by removal. Trade fixtures left behind after the lease ends may become the landlord's property through **[[accession]]**.

## Legal descriptions

A street address isn't precise enough to convey title. A deed needs a **[[legal description]]** that identifies exactly one parcel. There are three main methods.

### Metes and bounds

[[Metes and bounds]] is the oldest method. "Metes" are distances and directions; "bounds" are boundaries, often marked by **[[Monument|monuments]]** (fixed objects such as iron pins, trees, or roads). The description starts at a [[point of beginning]] (POB), runs around the parcel with courses and distances (for example, "north 45 degrees east, 200 feet"), and must **return to the [[POB]]**. A description that doesn't close is defective.

If a monument and a measured distance conflict, monuments generally control.

### Lot and block (recorded plat)

When a developer subdivides land, a surveyor prepares a **[[plat map]]** showing each lot and block, which is recorded with the county. A deed can then describe a parcel as "Lot 7, Block 3, Aspen Ridge Subdivision, according to the plat recorded in…" This [[lot and block]] method (also called the *recorded plat* system) is the most common description for urban and suburban homes.

### Rectangular (government) survey system

The [[rectangular survey system]], also called the Public Land Survey System, is used across most of the western and midwestern United States, including Colorado. Colorado descriptions are tied to three principal meridians: the **[[Principal meridian|Sixth Principal Meridian]]** (most of the state), the **[[Principal meridian|New Mexico Principal Meridian]]** (parts of southwestern and south-central Colorado), and the small **[[Principal meridian|Ute Meridian]]** near Grand Junction. It's built on a grid:

- **[[Principal meridian|Principal meridians]]** run north–south; **[[Base line|base lines]]** run east–west.
- **[[Range line|Range lines]]** run north–south every 6 miles; **[[Township line|township lines]]** run east–west every 6 miles.
- The squares they form are **[[Township|townships]]**, each 6 miles by 6 miles (36 square miles, or 23,040 acres). A block of 16 townships, 24 miles on a side, is sometimes called a **[[quadrangle]]**.
- Each [[township]] is divided into 36 **[[Section|sections]]**, numbered 1 through 36 in a back-and-forth (boustrophedon) pattern starting in the northeast corner: section 1 is in the northeast corner, section 6 in the northwest, section 36 in the southeast.
- A [[section]] is 1 mile by 1 mile, which is 1 square mile, or **640 acres**.

Because the earth is curved, the grid can't be perfect. **[[Correction line|Correction lines]]** (every 24 miles) and **[[Government lot|government lots]]** (irregular parcels along water or grid edges) handle the leftovers.

### Acreage math

To find acreage from a rectangular survey description, read the description **backward**, starting at the section, and divide 640 by each fraction's denominator.

Example: *"The NE 1/4 of the SW 1/4 of Section 12"*

- Section 12 = 640 acres
- SW 1/4 = 640 ÷ 4 = 160 acres
- NE 1/4 of that = 160 ÷ 4 = **40 acres**

Shortcut: multiply the denominators (4 × 4 = 16) and divide into 640: 640 ÷ 16 = 40.

If the description uses "and" (for example, "the N 1/2 of the NW 1/4 **and** the SE 1/4"), it describes two separate parcels. Compute each one and add them together.

> **Exam tip:** "N 1/2 of the NE 1/4 of the SE 1/4" = 640 ÷ (2 × 4 × 4) = 640 ÷ 32 = 20 acres. The more fractions in the description, the smaller the parcel.

## Land measurement facts to memorize

| Unit | Equals |
|---|---|
| 1 [[acre]] | 43,560 square feet |
| 1 mile | 5,280 feet |
| 1 square mile (section) | 640 acres |
| 1 township | 36 sections = 36 square miles |
| 1 rod | 16.5 feet |
| 1 square yard | 9 square feet |
| 1 acre | 4,840 square yards |

A quick conversion: a rectangular lot 330 feet by 660 feet is 217,800 sq ft ÷ 43,560 = 5 acres.

### Vertical descriptions

Condominium units and air rights need elevation, not just a footprint. Surveyors measure height from a **[[datum]]**, a reference point (often mean sea level or a local benchmark). A condo unit's description may refer to the recorded condominium map and declaration.

lessons.title: Estates and forms of ownership
lessons.body:
## Estates in land

An **[[estate]]** is the degree, quantity, and duration of an owner's interest in property. Estates fall into two families:

| Freehold estates (ownership) | Leasehold estates (tenancy) |
|---|---|
| Duration is indefinite or measured by a life | Duration is set by a lease |
| Owner holds title | Tenant holds possession; landlord keeps title |
| Fee simple, life estate | Estate for years, periodic, at will, at sufferance |

A [[freehold estate]] is an ownership interest; a [[leasehold estate]] is a tenant's right to possess property owned by someone else. Leaseholds are treated as personal property.

### Fee simple estates

- **[[Fee simple absolute]]** is the most complete ownership the law allows. It has no time limit, it can be sold or left by will, and it passes to heirs if the owner dies without a will. When people say someone "owns" a home, this is usually what they mean.
- **[[Fee simple defeasible]]** is fee ownership that can end if a stated condition happens or stops happening. There are two versions:
  - **[[Fee simple determinable]]** uses words of duration like "so long as" or "while." If the condition is broken, title returns to the grantor **automatically**. The grantor's future interest is a **[[possibility of reverter]]**.
  - **[[Fee simple subject to a condition subsequent]]** uses words like "on condition that" or "provided that." If the condition is broken, the grantor must **take action** to get the property back. The grantor's future interest is a **[[right of reentry]]** (power of termination).

> **Exam tip:** "So long as" = automatic reversion (determinable). "On condition that" = grantor must act (condition subsequent).

### Life estates

A **[[life estate]]** lasts for the life of a named person.

- In a **[[conventional life estate]]**, the measuring life is the life tenant's own. "To Ann for life."
- In a **[[life estate pur autre vie]]**, the measuring life is someone else's. "To Ann for the life of Bob." When Bob dies, Ann's estate ends.

When the life estate ends, the property goes to either:

- the grantor (or the grantor's heirs), which is a **[[reversion]]**, or
- a third party named in the deed, the **[[remainderman]]**, who holds a **[[remainder]]** interest.

The life tenant may live on the property, rent it out, or sell or mortgage the life estate, but can't convey more than they own. A buyer gets only an interest that ends at the measuring death. The life tenant must not commit **[[waste]]** (damage that lowers the value for the future owner) and generally pays property taxes and routine upkeep.

**[[Legal life estate|Legal life estates]]** are created by state law rather than by a deed. Historically these included dower and curtesy (a surviving spouse's interest), and many states have abolished them. **[[Homestead]]** laws in many states protect part of the value of a family home from certain creditors.

### Leasehold estates

| Type | Key feature |
|---|---|
| Estate for years | Fixed start and end date (even if shorter than a year); ends without notice |
| Periodic tenancy | Renews automatically each period (month-to-month); ends with proper notice |
| Tenancy at will | No set term; either party can end it; ends on the death of either party |
| Tenancy at sufferance | Tenant holds over without the landlord's consent after the lease ends |

## Forms of ownership

Estates describe *how much* is owned. Forms of ownership describe *who* holds it and how.

### Ownership in severalty

**[[Severalty]]** means one owner, a single person or a single legal entity such as a corporation. The name sounds like "several," which is a classic trap: it means the owner's interest is *severed* from everyone else's.

### Tenancy in common

In a **[[tenancy in common]]** (TIC):

- Each co-owner holds an **[[undivided interest]]**: each one may use the whole property and owns no particular square foot of it.
- The shares may be **unequal** (60/40, for example).
- Each owner can sell, mortgage, or leave their share by will **without the others' consent**.
- There is **no [[right of survivorship]]**. A deceased owner's share passes to their heirs or devisees.
- Only one unity is required: **[[Four unities|possession]]**.

Any co-owner can ask a court for a **[[partition]]** if co-owners can't agree. The court divides the property, or orders it sold and divides the proceeds.

### Joint tenancy

A **[[joint tenancy]]** has one defining feature: the **[[right of survivorship]]**. When a joint tenant dies, the deceased owner's interest passes to the surviving joint tenants automatically. It doesn't go through probate, and a joint tenant can't leave the interest by will.

Creating a joint tenancy traditionally requires the **[[four unities]]** (PITT):

- **P**ossession: equal right to possess the whole property
- **I**nterest: equal ownership shares
- **T**ime: interests acquired at the same time
- **T**itle: interests acquired by the same deed or will

If one joint tenant sells their interest, the buyer does **not** become a joint tenant. The buyer holds as a tenant in common with the remaining owners, who stay joint tenants with one another.

> **Exam tip:** A, B, and C are joint tenants. C sells to D. Now A and B are joint tenants with each other, and D is a tenant in common owning 1/3. If A dies, B owns 2/3 and D owns 1/3.

**Colorado note:** Under C.R.S. 38-31-101, when property is conveyed to two or more natural persons, Colorado presumes a tenancy in common unless the deed expressly declares a joint tenancy (for example, "as joint tenants," "in joint tenancy," or "JTWROS"). Only natural persons (and fiduciaries such as co-trustees) can hold as joint tenants in Colorado. Most states have a similar presumption favoring tenancy in common.

### Tenancy by the entirety

**[[Tenancy by the entirety]]** is a special form of co-ownership for married couples, recognized in some states. It works like joint tenancy (survivorship, the four unities plus the unity of marriage), but neither spouse can convey or encumber the property alone, and it's generally protected from creditors of only one spouse. Divorce ends it.

**Colorado note:** Colorado does **not** recognize tenancy by the entirety. C.R.S. 38-31-201 says no conveyance creates one, and a deed that tries to create one creates a joint tenancy instead.

### Community property

In **[[community property]]** states (a minority of states, mostly in the West and Southwest), property acquired during marriage generally belongs to both spouses equally, while property owned before marriage or received by gift or inheritance is **[[separate property]]**. Colorado is **not** a community property state. Colorado divides marital property at divorce by equitable distribution.

### Comparison table

| | Severalty | Tenancy in common | Joint tenancy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Number of owners | One | Two or more | Two or more |
| Shares | All | Can be unequal | Equal |
| Survivorship | n/a | No; goes to heirs | Yes; goes to survivors |
| Can owner sell share? | Yes | Yes | Yes, but it breaks the joint tenancy for that share |
| Unities required | n/a | Possession | Possession, interest, time, title |

## Special ownership arrangements

### Condominiums

In a **[[condominium]]**, each owner holds **[[Fee simple absolute|fee simple]] title to an individual unit** (generally the airspace inside the walls) plus an **[[undivided interest]], as a [[Tenancy in common|tenant in common]], in the common elements** (hallways, roof, grounds, pool). Some areas are **[[limited common elements]]** reserved for one unit, such as an assigned parking space or a balcony. A recorded **[[declaration]]** creates the condominium, and an owners' association manages it, funded by assessments. Unpaid assessments can become a lien on the unit.

### Cooperatives

In a **[[cooperative]]** (co-op), a corporation owns the building. Residents buy **shares of stock** in the corporation and receive a **[[proprietary lease]]** for their unit. Because the buyer owns stock rather than real estate, a co-op interest is usually treated as **[[personal property]]**. The co-op board often must approve buyers. If other shareholders stop paying their share of building costs, a blanket mortgage default can endanger everyone.

### Timeshares

A **[[timeshare]]** divides use of a property by time:

- A **[[timeshare estate]]** conveys a fee interest for a recurring period (for example, week 22 every year).
- A **[[timeshare use]]** (right-to-use) is a contractual or lease-type right to use the property for a period, without real property ownership.

### Trusts

In a **[[trust]]**, a **[[trustor]]** (also called the settlor or grantor) conveys property to a **[[trustee]]**, who holds legal title and manages it for a **[[beneficiary]]**. Common types include living (inter vivos) trusts, testamentary trusts (created by a will), and land trusts (where the beneficiary often keeps control and the trust keeps the beneficiary's identity private).

### Business ownership

- **[[Corporation]]:** a separate legal entity that holds title in severalty. Shareholders have limited liability, but a C corporation's income is taxed at the corporate level and again as dividends ("double taxation").
- **[[General partnership]]:** all partners share management and unlimited liability.
- **[[Limited partnership]]:** at least one general partner manages and has unlimited liability; limited partners are passive investors whose liability is limited to their investment.
- **[[Limited liability company]] ([[LLC]]):** members get limited liability with flexible, pass-through tax treatment. LLCs are popular for holding investment property.
- **[[Syndicate]] / [[joint venture]]:** a group pooling money for one investment or project. These are arrangements, not separate legal forms, and are often organized as partnerships or LLCs.
- **[[Real estate investment trust]] ([[REIT]]):** a company that pools investors' money to own or finance real estate and, if it meets federal tax rules, avoids corporate income tax on the income it distributes to owners. The key tests: at least **100 owners**, no more than half owned by five or fewer individuals, at least **75% of gross income** from real-estate sources such as rents and mortgage interest, and at least **90% of taxable income** paid out to owners each year. (Older textbooks say 95%; the requirement dropped to 90% in 2001.)

> **Exam tip:** When a buyer gives up management control for a passive return, such as a condo unit that must go into a mandatory rental pool, the deal can be a **[[security]]**. Selling securities takes a securities license and registration, not just a real estate license.

lessons.title: Encumbrances: liens, easements, encroachments, and adverse possession
lessons.body:
## What an encumbrance is

An **[[encumbrance]]** is any claim, right, or interest held by someone other than the owner that lowers the property's value or limits its use. Encumbrances don't necessarily stop a sale, but the buyer takes the property subject to them unless they're cleared.

There are two broad groups:

- **Money claims:** liens.
- **Physical or use limits:** easements, encroachments, deed restrictions.

## Liens

A **[[lien]]** is a creditor's claim against property as security for a debt. If the debt isn't paid, the creditor can force a sale of the property (foreclose) to collect.

### Classifying liens

| Classification | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Voluntary | Owner chooses to create it | Mortgage, deed of trust |
| Involuntary | Created by law without the owner's consent | Tax lien, judgment lien, mechanic's lien |
| Specific | Attaches to one particular property | Mortgage, property tax, special assessment, mechanic's lien |
| General | Attaches to all of a debtor's property in the area | Judgment lien, federal income tax lien, estate/inheritance tax lien |

A mortgage, then, is **voluntary and specific**. A judgment lien is **involuntary and general**.

### Common liens

- **[[Mortgage]] / [[deed of trust]] lien:** secures a loan used to buy or refinance the property.
- **[[Property tax lien]]:** created by law for unpaid ad valorem taxes.
- **[[Special assessment|Special assessment lien]]:** for public improvements that benefit specific properties.
- **[[Mechanic's lien]]:** protects contractors, subcontractors, and suppliers who improved the property and weren't paid. In many states its priority can date back to when work began or materials were first delivered, not to when the lien was filed. That's why title insurers worry about recent construction.
- **[[Judgment lien]]:** a court judgment against a person becomes a general lien on that person's real property in the county where it's recorded.
- **[[Federal tax lien|Federal tax liens]]:** for unpaid federal income or estate taxes.

### Lien priority

The basic rule is **[[Lien priority|first in time, first in right]]**: liens rank by the date and time they were recorded. The big exception is that **property tax and special assessment liens generally take priority over all other liens**, no matter when they were recorded.

A lender with an earlier lien can agree to move behind a later lien by signing a **[[subordination]] agreement**. This often happens when a landowner's existing loan is subordinated to a construction loan.

> **Exam tip:** A seller has a 2019 mortgage, a 2023 judgment lien, and unpaid property taxes for this year. On a foreclosure sale, the property taxes get paid first, then the mortgage, then the judgment.

## Easements

An **[[easement]]** is a right to use another person's land for a specific purpose, such as a driveway, utility line, or path to a lake. An easement is a non-possessory interest in land: the holder may use the land but doesn't own it or possess it.

### Easement appurtenant

An **[[easement appurtenant]]** involves two parcels:

- The **[[dominant tenement]]** (dominant estate) is the parcel that *benefits* from the easement.
- The **[[servient tenement]]** (servient estate) is the parcel that *carries the burden*, the land that is crossed.

An easement appurtenant **[[runs with the land]]**. If either parcel is sold, the easement continues: the new owner of the dominant parcel keeps the right, and the new owner of the servient parcel takes subject to it.

### Easement in gross

An **[[easement in gross]]** has a servient tenement but **no [[dominant tenement]]**. It benefits a person or company rather than a neighboring parcel.

- **Commercial** easements in gross (utility lines, pipelines, railroad rights-of-way) are usually transferable.
- **Personal** easements in gross (a right for one individual to fish on a pond, for example) usually can't be sold or transferred, and they end when that person dies.

### How easements are created

- **[[Express easement|Express grant or reservation]]:** written in a deed or separate agreement.
- **[[Easement by necessity]]:** created by law when a parcel is sold with no access to a road (landlocked) and the parcels were once under common ownership.
- **[[Easement by implication]]:** implied from the circumstances and prior use when land is divided.
- **[[Prescriptive easement]]:** acquired by using someone else's land openly, continuously, and without permission for the period set by state law. It's similar to adverse possession, but it gains a *right to use*, not ownership.
- **[[Condemnation]]:** a government or utility acquires an easement through eminent domain.
- **[[Party wall]]:** a shared wall on a property line, with each owner holding an easement in the half owned by the other.

### How easements end

- **[[Merger]]:** one person comes to own both the dominant and servient parcels.
- **[[Release]]:** the dominant owner releases it in writing (often by quitclaim deed).
- **[[Abandonment]]:** the holder intentionally gives it up, shown by conduct, not just non-use.
- **Purpose ends:** an easement by necessity ends when another access road is built.
- **Non-use** of a prescriptive easement for the statutory period, in some states.

## Licenses

A **[[license]]** is **personal, revocable permission** to enter someone's land for a specific purpose, such as a ticket to a concert, permission to hunt, or a neighbor letting you park in a driveway. A license is **not** an interest in land, it doesn't run with the land, and it can generally be revoked at any time. It ends when either party dies or the land is sold.

> **Exam tip:** Easement = interest in land, usually in writing, not easily revoked. License = personal privilege, revocable, no interest in land.

## Encroachments

An **[[encroachment]]** happens when an improvement on one property extends onto a neighbor's land or into a setback or easement area. Examples include a fence 3 feet over the line, a garage built partly on the next lot, or roof eaves hanging over the boundary.

- Encroachments are usually discovered by a **[[survey]]**. A standard title insurance policy generally doesn't cover them (see the transfer-of-title lesson).
- Left alone long enough, an encroachment can lead to a claim of adverse possession or a prescriptive easement.
- The neighbor's remedies include a lawsuit for removal (an injunction) or damages.

## Adverse possession

**[[Adverse possession]]** is a way to gain **[[title]]** to someone else's land by occupying it for the period set by state law. It is a form of **[[involuntary alienation]]** for the record owner.

The possession must generally be:

- **O**pen and
- **N**otorious (visible, so the true owner could discover it)
- **C**ontinuous for the statutory period
- **E**xclusive (not shared with the owner or the public)
- **A**dverse, also called hostile (without the owner's permission)

Many students remember these as **OCEAN** or **ONCEA**. Permission defeats a claim: a tenant or someone with a license can't adversely possess, because their use isn't hostile.

**[[Tacking]]:** in many states, successive adverse possessors who are in **[[privity]]** (for example, a buyer who takes over from a seller) can add their periods together to reach the statutory time.

To get marketable record title, the adverse possessor usually files a **[[quiet title action]]**.

**Colorado note:** Under C.R.S. 38-41-101, the period in Colorado is **18 years**. In fee-title cases filed on or after July 1, 2008, the claimant must prove each element by **[[clear and convincing evidence]]**. Where title would vest on or after that date, the claimant must also show that the claimant (or a predecessor) had a **reasonable, good-faith belief** that they were the actual owner. The court may also order the successful claimant to compensate the former owner. Adverse possession doesn't run against state or local government land. Statutory periods vary widely among states, so the national exam usually asks about elements rather than a specific number of years.

## Deed restrictions as encumbrances

Private restrictions recorded in a deed or a subdivision declaration are also encumbrances. They limit what an owner may build or do. These are covered with land use controls in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Land use controls: public and private
lessons.body:
## Public and private controls

An owner's rights aren't unlimited. Land use is shaped by:

- **Public controls:** government powers over private property.
- **Private controls:** restrictions created by owners and developers through deeds and recorded declarations.

## The four government powers (PETE)

Government's rights over private land are summarized as **PETE**:

| Power | What it does | Compensation? |
|---|---|---|
| **P**olice power | Regulates use for public health, safety, morals, and welfare | No |
| **E**minent domain | Takes private property for public use | Yes, just compensation |
| **T**axation | Levies taxes and special assessments, enforced by liens | n/a |
| **E**scheat | Takes property when an owner dies with no will and no heirs | No |

### Police power

**[[Police power]]** is the government's authority to regulate property use to protect the public. It's the source of zoning, building codes, subdivision rules, environmental regulations, and rent controls. Regulation under the police power doesn't require compensation, as long as it doesn't go so far that it effectively takes the property.

### Eminent domain

**[[Eminent domain]]** is the government's power to take private property for **[[public use]]** with **[[just compensation]]** (usually fair market value). **[[Condemnation]]** is the legal process used to exercise it. Governments and certain entities with delegated authority (utilities, for example) can use it to build roads, schools, pipelines, or power lines.

- The owner can challenge whether the use is public or whether the payment is fair, but generally can't stop a valid taking.
- **[[Inverse condemnation]]** is a lawsuit an *owner* brings when government action has effectively taken or damaged the property (for example, an airport's flight path) without a formal condemnation.
- A partial taking may include **[[severance damages]]** for the drop in value of the remaining land.

### Taxation

Local governments levy **[[ad valorem]]** (by value) property taxes, which become a specific lien on the property. A **[[special assessment]]** is a charge against only the properties that benefit from a specific public improvement, such as new sidewalks, sewer lines, or street paving. Special assessments are specific, involuntary liens, and like property taxes they generally have priority over other liens.

### Escheat

**[[Escheat]]** transfers property to the state (or county) when an owner dies **without a will and without heirs**. It also applies to some abandoned property. Escheat keeps property from becoming ownerless.

## Planning and zoning

Cities and counties usually adopt a **[[comprehensive plan]]** (master plan) for future growth. They then carry it out through **[[zoning]]** ordinances, which divide land into districts and set the allowed uses in each. States give local governments this authority through **[[Enabling act|enabling acts]]**.

Zoning ordinances commonly regulate:

- **Use:** residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, mixed-use, planned unit development (PUD).
- **Density:** units per acre, minimum lot size.
- **Bulk and placement:** building height, lot coverage, **[[Setback|setbacks]]** from lot lines, floor-area ratio.
- **Aesthetics:** historic districts, signage.

Related concepts:

- **[[Buffer zone]]:** a strip (such as a park or a light-use district) separating incompatible uses, like homes and heavy industry.
- **[[Cumulative zoning]]** allows "higher" uses in a "lower" zone (a home in a commercial zone). **[[Exclusive zoning]]** allows only the listed use.
- **[[Downzoning]]:** rezoning to a less intense use (commercial to residential, for example).
- **[[Spot zoning]]:** rezoning a single parcel in a way that benefits one owner and conflicts with the comprehensive plan. It is often struck down as illegal.
- **[[Rezoning]] (amendment):** changing the zoning of an area through the legislative process.

### Exceptions to zoning

These three show up on almost every exam:

**[[Nonconforming use]]:** a use that was legal when it started but doesn't fit a newer zoning ordinance. It is usually allowed to continue ("grandfathered"). Common limits: the owner usually can't expand it, and if the structure is destroyed or the use is abandoned for a certain time, the right to continue may be lost.

**[[Variance]]:** permission to depart from the *strict requirements* of the ordinance, usually physical standards such as setbacks, height, or lot coverage, because applying them would cause an **unusual hardship** tied to the property (an odd lot shape or steep slope, for example). The hardship can't be self-created, and a variance generally can't be used to bring in a use the zone doesn't allow.

**[[Conditional use permit]]** (also called a *special use permit* or *special exception*): permission for a use the ordinance **lists as allowed if conditions are met**, because it serves the community. Examples include a church, school, or hospital in a residential zone. The approval comes with conditions (parking, hours, landscaping).

| Tool | Why it's granted | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Nonconforming use | Use existed before the rule | Corner store in an area later zoned residential |
| Variance | Hardship from strict rules | Reduced setback on an irregular lot |
| Conditional use | Ordinance allows it with conditions | Church in a residential zone |

> **Exam tip:** "Existed first" = nonconforming use. "Hardship" = variance. "Public benefit, with conditions" = conditional use.

Zoning decisions are typically made by a planning commission and a **[[board of adjustment]]** (zoning board of appeals), which hears variance requests and appeals.

## Building codes

**[[Building codes]]** set minimum construction standards for structure, plumbing, electrical, fire safety, and energy use. They're enforced through **[[Building permit|building permits]]** and inspections. When the work passes final inspection, the building department issues a **[[certificate of occupancy]]**, which allows people to legally occupy the building. When a zoning rule and a building code (or any two rules) conflict, the **stricter** standard generally controls.

## Subdivision regulations

When a developer divides raw land into lots, local subdivision regulations control street layout and width, utilities, drainage, lot size, open space, and dedication of land for public use. The developer submits a **[[plat]]** for approval and records it, which creates the lot-and-block legal descriptions. Developers may also have to pay **[[Impact fee|impact fees]]** to fund the schools, parks, and roads new growth requires.

At the federal level, the **[[Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act]]** requires developers who sell or lease certain unimproved lots through interstate commerce to register with the federal government and give buyers a **[[property report]]** before they sign, unless an exemption applies. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) administers it. A buyer of a covered lot can generally revoke the contract until midnight of the seventh day after signing, and subdivisions of fewer than 25 lots are exempt from the act.

## Environmental regulation (brief)

Federal and state laws address hazards such as lead-based paint, asbestos, radon, underground storage tanks, and contaminated land. Under the federal Superfund law (CERCLA), the current owner or operator, and anyone who owned or operated the site when hazardous waste was disposed of there, can be liable for cleanup costs. Liability is strict (fault doesn't matter), joint and several, and retroactive, which is why commercial buyers order environmental site assessments. Disclosure duties are covered in other modules.

## Private controls

### Deed restrictions and covenants

A **[[deed restriction]]** limits how a buyer may use the property. A grantor writes it into a deed, or a developer records it for a whole subdivision. Restrictions can be:

- **[[Covenant|Covenants]]:** promises. If one is broken, the remedy is usually a court order (an **[[injunction]]**) or damages.
- **[[Condition|Conditions]]:** if broken, the grantor may be able to reclaim title (see fee simple defeasible). Courts dislike forfeiture, so they interpret restrictions as covenants when they can.

Restrictions that discriminate based on race or other protected classes are **unenforceable** under fair housing law and court decisions, even if they're still in old recorded documents.

### CC&Rs and HOAs

In most planned communities and condominiums, the developer records a declaration of **[[CC&Rs]]** (covenants, conditions, and restrictions) that binds every lot. CC&Rs typically cover architectural approval, fences, paint colors, pets, parking, rentals, and maintenance. They **[[run with the land]]** and bind later buyers who take with constructive notice from the recorded declaration.

A **[[homeowners' association]]** (HOA) enforces the CC&Rs, maintains common areas, and charges **[[assessments]]** (regular dues and special assessments). Unpaid assessments can become a lien on the owner's property.

A neighbor or the HOA can enforce restrictions by seeking an **[[injunction]]**. If they wait too long, the court may refuse to enforce the restriction under the doctrine of **[[laches]]** (unreasonable delay). Restrictions may also end by their own terms, by agreement of the owners, or when conditions in the neighborhood change enough that the restriction no longer makes sense.

> **Exam tip:** When a private restriction and a public law both apply, the **more restrictive** one generally governs. A zoning ordinance allowing 35-foot buildings doesn't override CC&Rs limiting homes to one story.

Colorado has its own common-interest community statute (CCIOA) with HOA rules. Those are covered in the state portion of this course.

lessons.title: Transfer of title: deeds, title insurance, recording, and foreclosure
lessons.body:
## How title changes hands

**[[Title]]** is ownership, and the evidence of ownership. **[[Alienation]]** is any transfer of title.

| Voluntary alienation | Involuntary alienation |
|---|---|
| Sale or gift by **[[deed]]** | **[[Descent]]** under intestacy laws |
| Transfer by **[[will]]** (devise) | **[[Escheat]]** to the state |
| | **[[Eminent domain]]** |
| | **[[Foreclosure]]** and tax sales |
| | **[[Adverse possession]]** |
| | Natural forces: **[[accretion]]** (land added slowly by water deposits), **[[erosion]]**, avulsion |

**[[Involuntary alienation]]** is a transfer of title without the owner's consent.

## Deeds

A **[[deed]]** is the written document that conveys title to real property from the **[[grantor]]** (the person giving title) to the **[[grantee]]** (the person receiving it).

### Requirements for a valid deed

- **In writing**, as the statute of frauds requires
- A **competent [[grantor]]** (legal age and sound mind)
- A **[[grantee]]** who can be identified (the grantee doesn't need to be competent; a minor can receive title)
- A recital of **[[consideration]]** ("for ten dollars and other good and valuable consideration"). A gift deed is valid too.
- A **[[granting clause]]** with words of conveyance ("grants," "conveys")
- An adequate **[[legal description]]**
- The **grantor's signature** (the grantee usually doesn't sign)
- **[[Delivery and acceptance]]**: title passes when the deed is delivered to and accepted by the grantee during the grantor's lifetime

Some deeds also include a **[[habendum clause]]** ("to have and to hold"), which defines the estate granted, and exceptions and reservations (for example, reserving mineral rights).

**[[Acknowledgment]]** is a formal declaration before a notary or other authorized officer that the signature is genuine and voluntary. In most states it isn't needed for a deed to be *valid* between the parties, but it's required to **[[Recording|record]]** the deed. (Colorado's statute, C.R.S. 38-35-106, is more forgiving: a recorded instrument gives notice even if the acknowledgment is missing or defective. In practice, Colorado deeds are still notarized.)

> **Exam tip:** Title passes on **[[delivery and acceptance]]**, not when the deed is signed and not when it's recorded. A deed found in a desk drawer after the grantor's death was never delivered and doesn't convey title.

### Types of deeds

| Deed | Warranties given | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **[[General warranty deed]]** | The most protection. Grantor warrants title against defects **at any time**, including before the grantor owned it | Standard sale where the buyer wants full protection |
| **[[Special warranty deed]]** | Grantor warrants only against defects arising **while the grantor owned** the property | Corporate sellers, lenders selling REO property, some fiduciaries |
| **[[Bargain and sale deed]]** | Implies the grantor holds title; gives no express warranties against encumbrances (in some states with limited covenants) | Tax sales, some foreclosures |
| **[[Quitclaim deed]]** | **No warranties.** Conveys whatever interest the grantor has, if any | Clearing a cloud on title, releasing an interest, transfers between family members or after divorce |
| **[[Personal representative's deed]]** | Fiduciary deed from an estate | Selling a deceased person's property through probate |

The usual covenants in a general warranty deed are:

- **[[Seisin]]:** the grantor owns the property and has the right to convey it.
- **[[Covenant against encumbrances|Against encumbrances]]:** there are no encumbrances except those listed.
- **[[Quiet enjoyment]]:** no one with a better title will disturb the grantee's possession.
- **[[Further assurance]]:** the grantor will sign any papers needed to perfect the title.
- **[[Warranty forever]]:** the grantor will defend the title against lawful claims.

Other fiduciary and court deeds include the **[[trustee's deed]]** (from a trustee), **[[sheriff's deed]]** (after a court-ordered sale), and **[[Guardian's deed|guardian's]]** or **[[Conservator's deed|conservator's deeds]]**. Fiduciary deeds generally carry only limited warranties. Colorado's Commission-approved deed forms include warranty, special warranty, bargain and sale, and quitclaim deeds.

> **Exam tip:** A quitclaim deed conveys the grantor's interest, if any. It does **not** promise the grantor owns anything. That's what makes it the go-to tool for removing a [[cloud on title]].

## Recording and notice

**[[Recording]]** means filing a deed, mortgage, lien, or other document with the county recorder (the county clerk and recorder in Colorado). Recording isn't required for a deed to be valid between grantor and grantee, but it protects the grantee against later claimants.

- **[[Constructive notice]]:** what the law presumes everyone knows, because it's in the public records or could be found by inspecting the property. A buyer is charged with knowing about recorded documents and about the rights of anyone in possession.
- **[[Actual notice]]:** what a person really knows, whether because they saw it, were told it, or read it.

States use different recording statutes to settle conflicts between two buyers of the same property:

- **[[Race statute|Race]]:** the first to record wins.
- **[[Notice statute|Notice]]:** a later buyer without notice of the earlier deed wins.
- **[[Race-notice]]:** a later buyer wins only if they had no notice **and** recorded first.

**Colorado note:** C.R.S. 38-35-109 describes Colorado's statute as a race-notice recording statute.

## Evidence of title

- **[[Chain of title]]:** the sequence of recorded conveyances from the original source of title to the current owner. A missing link is a **[[Gap in title|gap]]** in the chain.
- **[[Abstract of title]]:** a condensed history of all recorded documents affecting the property. It's not insurance; an attorney reads it and gives an **[[attorney's opinion of title]]**.
- **[[Title insurance]]:** a policy that pays for covered losses from title defects. The insurer issues a **[[title commitment]]** before closing, listing requirements to be met and exceptions the policy won't cover.

**[[Marketable title]]** is title free enough from reasonable doubt that a prudent buyer would accept it. It doesn't have to be perfect, but it shouldn't expose the buyer to likely lawsuits. Purchase contracts usually require the seller to deliver marketable title. A **[[cloud on title]]** (an old unreleased mortgage, a possible heir's claim) can be removed by a quitclaim deed from the claimant or by a **[[quiet title action]]**.

### Owner's vs. lender's title policies

| | Owner's policy | Lender's (loan) policy |
|---|---|---|
| Protects | The buyer/owner | The lender |
| Amount | Usually the purchase price | Usually the loan amount; coverage drops as the loan is paid down |
| Duration | As long as the insured or their heirs hold an interest | Until the loan is paid off |
| Premium | One-time, paid at closing | One-time, paid at closing |

### Standard vs. extended coverage

- **[[Standard coverage]]** protects against defects in the public records plus certain hidden risks such as forgery, a grantor's incompetence, improper delivery, and undisclosed heirs. It usually **excludes** matters that only an inspection or survey would reveal: **rights of parties in possession**, boundary disputes and **[[encroachments]]**, **unrecorded easements**, and **unrecorded mechanic's liens**.
- **[[Extended coverage]]** removes some or all of those standard exceptions, usually after a survey and inspection.

No policy covers defects the insured created or already knew about, or government regulations like zoning.

## Closing basics

At **[[closing]]** (settlement), the buyer pays the purchase price, the seller delivers the deed, liens are paid off, the new loan is funded, and documents are recorded. Closing is commonly handled by a **[[Closing company|settlement agent]]**, such as a title company, escrow agent, or attorney. A **[[closing statement]]** accounts for every debit and credit, including **[[prorations]]** of taxes, rents, and HOA dues. Colorado closing practice is covered in the state portion of this course.

## Foreclosure and alternatives

A **[[foreclosure]]** is the legal process a lender uses to sell a property to satisfy a defaulted loan.

- **[[Judicial foreclosure]]:** the lender sues, and a court orders a sale (often conducted by a sheriff).
- **[[Nonjudicial foreclosure]]:** a **[[power of sale]]** in the deed of trust allows a trustee to sell without a lawsuit. Colorado uses a **[[public trustee]]** system for most deed-of-trust foreclosures (details in the state module).
- **[[Equity of redemption]]:** the borrower's right to pay off the debt and stop the foreclosure *before* the sale.
- **[[Statutory redemption]]:** a right some states give to buy the property back *after* the sale for a set period.
- **[[Deficiency judgment]]:** if the sale brings less than the debt, the lender may be able to get a personal judgment for the shortfall, where state law allows.

Alternatives:

- **[[Deed in lieu of foreclosure]]:** the borrower voluntarily deeds the property to the lender. The lender takes title subject to junior liens, so lenders often refuse it when other liens exist.
- **[[Short sale]]:** the property sells for less than the loan balance, and the **lender agrees** to accept the net proceeds as payment. Lender approval is essential, and the lender may or may not release the borrower from the remaining balance.

## Wills, probate, and intestacy

- A **[[will]]** lets a person (the **[[testator]]**) direct how property passes at death. Real property left by will is a **[[devise]]**, and the recipient is a **[[devisee]]**. A **[[codicil]]** amends a will.
- **[[Probate]]** is the court-supervised process of proving a will, paying debts, and distributing property. The court appoints a **[[personal representative]]** (also called an executor if named in the will, or an administrator if there's no will) who can sell estate property with a personal representative's deed.
- A person who dies without a valid will dies **[[intestate]]**. State **[[intestate succession]]** (descent) statutes decide which relatives inherit. If there are no heirs, the property **[[Escheat|escheats]]** to the state.
- Property held in **[[joint tenancy]]** passes to the surviving joint tenants outside probate, and property in a trust passes under the trust terms.

> **Exam tip:** "Testate" means with a will (property passes by devise). "Intestate" means without a will (property passes by descent). No will and no heirs means escheat.

questions.stem: A seller removes a built-in, wall-mounted bookcase that was custom-made to fit the living room alcove before the buyer moves in. The purchase contract didn't mention the bookcase. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The bookcase was personal property because it could be removed with hand tools
The bookcase was a fixture, so it should have stayed with the house
The bookcase was a trade fixture belonging to the seller
Ownership of the bookcase depends only on what the seller intended when it was built
questions.explanation: Attachment and adaptation (custom-built for that alcove) make the bookcase a fixture, which transfers with the real estate unless the contract excludes it. Trade fixtures belong to tenants who use them in a business, not to homeowner-sellers.

questions.stem: How many acres are in the SE 1/4 of the NW 1/4 of a section?
questions.explanation: A section is 640 acres. 640 ÷ 4 = 160 acres for the NW 1/4, and 160 ÷ 4 = 40 acres for the SE 1/4 of that.

questions.stem: Which legal description method requires that the description return to its point of beginning?
questions.explanation: A metes and bounds description begins at a point of beginning and follows courses and distances around the parcel, and it must close at the point of beginning to be valid.

questions.stem: A restaurant tenant installed commercial ovens and a walk-in cooler bolted to the floor. When the lease ends, these items are generally
choices: the landlord's property because they are bolted to the building
real property that would pass to a buyer if the building were sold
the landlord's property unless the lease specifically says otherwise
the tenant's personal property, removable before the lease ends
questions.explanation: Equipment a tenant installs for business use is a trade fixture and stays the tenant's personal property. The tenant must remove it by the end of the lease and repair any damage from removal.

questions.stem: Andre, Bea, and Carl own a property as joint tenants. Carl sells his interest to Dana. Then Andre dies. Who owns the property, and how?
choices: Bea owns 2/3 and Dana owns 1/3 as tenants in common
Bea and Dana each own 1/2 as joint tenants
Bea owns 1/3, Dana owns 1/3, and Andre's heirs own 1/3
Bea owns the entire property by right of survivorship
questions.explanation: Dana's purchase broke the joint tenancy only as to Carl's share, so Dana holds 1/3 as a tenant in common. Andre and Bea stayed joint tenants, so Andre's 1/3 passed to Bea by survivorship, leaving Bea with 2/3.

questions.stem: Which of the four unities is the ONLY one required for a tenancy in common?
questions.explanation: Tenants in common need only unity of possession: each may use the whole property. Their shares can be unequal and acquired at different times through different deeds.

questions.stem: A deed conveys land to a church "so long as the property is used for religious purposes." What estate did the church receive?
choices: Fee simple subject to a condition subsequent
questions.explanation: "So long as" is the language of duration that creates a fee simple determinable. If the use stops, title reverts to the grantor automatically under the possibility of reverter. "On condition that" would point to a condition subsequent.

questions.stem: Maria grants a life estate to her brother Leo, with the property to pass to her niece Rosa when Leo dies. What is Rosa's interest?
questions.explanation: A third party named to receive the property when a life estate ends is the remainderman, holding a remainder interest. A reversion would mean the property returns to Maria or her heirs.

questions.stem: A buyer purchases a unit in a building and receives shares of stock in the corporation that owns the building plus a proprietary lease. What type of ownership is this?
questions.explanation: In a co-op, a corporation owns the building and residents own shares plus a proprietary lease, so the interest is usually treated as personal property. Condo owners hold fee title to their units.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a specific, involuntary lien?
questions.explanation: A property tax lien attaches only to the taxed parcel (specific) and arises by law (involuntary). A mortgage is voluntary; judgment and federal income tax liens are general liens.

questions.stem: Owner A's lot has a recorded right to use a driveway across neighbor B's lot to reach the street. A sells to C. Which statement is correct?
choices: The easement ended at the sale because easements are personal
C may use the driveway only after getting B's new written consent
The easement runs with the land, so C may use the driveway
B's lot is now the dominant tenement and C's lot is servient
questions.explanation: An easement appurtenant benefits the dominant parcel (A's lot, now C's) and burdens the servient parcel (B's lot). It runs with the land and transfers automatically when either parcel is sold.

questions.stem: A neighbor gives a friend verbal permission to fish in his pond on weekends. What does the friend have?
questions.explanation: Personal, revocable permission to enter land for a specific purpose is a license, not an interest in land. It can be revoked at any time and ends when the land is sold or either party dies.

questions.stem: Which element must an adverse possessor generally prove?
choices: Possession was with the owner's permission throughout
Possession was shared with the owner and the public
Possession was kept hidden so the owner wouldn't object
Possession was hostile, open, and continuous
questions.explanation: Adverse possession requires open, notorious, continuous, exclusive, and hostile (adverse) possession for the statutory period. Permission defeats the hostility element, and shared or hidden use fails exclusivity and notoriety.

questions.stem: A gas station has operated on a corner for 30 years. The city rezones the area as residential only. The station may most likely keep operating as a
questions.explanation: A use that was legal before a new zoning ordinance is generally allowed to continue as a nonconforming (grandfathered) use. A variance relieves hardship from the ordinance's requirements; it isn't needed for a use that existed first.

questions.stem: An owner's lot is an irregular triangle, and meeting the required 25-foot side setback would leave almost no buildable area. What should the owner request?
questions.explanation: A variance allows a departure from an ordinance's physical requirements, such as setbacks, when strict enforcement would cause an unusual hardship from conditions of the property itself.

questions.stem: A state highway department needs part of a farm to widen a road. The owner refuses to sell. The state can acquire the land through
questions.explanation: Eminent domain lets government take private property for public use with just compensation, through condemnation. Police power regulates use without taking ownership.

questions.stem: A homeowner dies without a will and with no living heirs. What happens to the home?
choices: It passes to the county by eminent domain
It goes to the mortgage lender
It is sold at a tax sale
questions.explanation: Escheat transfers property to the state when an owner dies intestate with no heirs. Eminent domain is a taking for public use with compensation.

questions.stem: A city installs new sidewalks and charges the cost only to owners of the lots that front the new sidewalks. This charge is a
questions.explanation: A special assessment charges the cost of a public improvement to the properties that benefit from it. It becomes a specific lien on each assessed lot.

questions.stem: Zoning allows homes up to 35 feet tall, but the subdivision's recorded CC&Rs limit homes to one story. A lot owner wants to build a two-story home. Which rule controls?
choices: The zoning ordinance, because public law overrides private restrictions
Neither, because the two rules conflict and cancel out
The CC&Rs, because the more restrictive rule generally governs
questions.explanation: When private restrictions and public regulations both apply, the stricter one generally controls. The zoning ordinance permits 35 feet but doesn't require it, so the owner can't violate the one-story CC&R.

questions.stem: Which government power is the basis for zoning ordinances and building codes?
questions.explanation: Police power lets government regulate property use to protect public health, safety, and welfare. It is the basis for zoning, building codes, and subdivision regulations, and requires no compensation.

questions.stem: At what point does title pass from grantor to grantee under a deed?
choices: When the grantor signs the deed in front of a witness
When the deed is delivered and accepted
When the deed is acknowledged before a notary public
When the deed is recorded with the county
questions.explanation: Title passes on delivery and acceptance during the grantor's lifetime. Recording gives constructive notice and protects the grantee, and acknowledgment is needed to record, but neither one transfers title.

questions.stem: Which deed gives the grantee the greatest protection?
choices: Bargain and sale deed with covenants
questions.explanation: A general warranty deed warrants title against defects arising at any time, including before the grantor owned the property. A special warranty deed covers only the grantor's period of ownership.

questions.stem: A title search turns up an old recorded document suggesting a former owner's relative may hold an interest in the property. The claim may or may not be valid. What is the simplest way to remove this cloud on title?
choices: Have the relative sign a quitclaim deed
Have the seller sign a general warranty deed
Buy an owner's policy with standard coverage
Record the buyer's deed before closing
questions.explanation: A quitclaim deed releases whatever interest the relative may have without any warranties, which clears the cloud. A quiet title action is the court alternative if the relative won't sign.

questions.stem: A buyer's standard-coverage owner's title policy would most likely NOT cover a loss caused by
choices: a forged deed earlier in the chain of title
an encroachment that only a survey would have revealed
a recorded lien the title company missed
a deed signed by a grantor who was legally incompetent
questions.explanation: Standard coverage excludes matters only a survey or inspection would reveal, such as encroachments, boundary disputes, and rights of parties in possession. Forgery, incompetence, and missed recorded liens are typical covered risks.

questions.stem: A buyer didn't inspect a property before closing. After closing, she learns a tenant in possession holds an unrecorded lease. Which statement is correct?
choices: The buyer takes free of the lease because it was never recorded
The buyer had actual notice of the lease at closing
The tenant must leave because the buyer's deed was recorded
The buyer has constructive notice because of the tenant's possession
questions.explanation: Constructive notice includes what a reasonable inspection would reveal, including the rights of people in possession. The buyer is treated as knowing about the tenant's lease even though she never saw it.

questions.stem: A seller owes $310,000 on a home that will sell for $280,000. The lender agrees to accept the net sale proceeds to release its lien. This is a
questions.explanation: In a short sale, the property sells for less than the loan balance and the lender agrees to accept the proceeds. In a deed in lieu, the borrower deeds the property directly to the lender.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of involuntary alienation?
choices: Conveyance of land by special warranty deed to a buyer
Gift of a cabin to a child by a quitclaim deed
Transfer of a family farm to a son by will
Loss of land to a neighbor by adverse possession
questions.explanation: Involuntary alienation transfers title without the owner's consent, as with adverse possession, foreclosure, eminent domain, escheat, and descent. Deeds and wills are voluntary alienation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is required in most states to record a deed but is generally NOT required for the deed to be valid between the parties?
questions.explanation: Acknowledgment (a declaration before a notary) makes a deed eligible for recording. The grantor's signature, legal description, and granting clause are essential to a valid deed.

cards.back: Real estate = land plus permanent improvements. Real property = real estate plus the bundle of legal rights of ownership.
Possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, and disposition.
By a bill of sale, not a deed.

Method of attachment, Adaptability, Relationship of parties, Intention, Agreement. A written agreement overrides the others; courts treat intention as the key test (some prep courses key method of attachment).
Business equipment a tenant installs. It stays the tenant's personal property and must be removed before the lease ends.
Annual crops planted by labor. They're personal property; a tenant farmer may return to harvest them after the lease ends, if the tenant didn't cause the lease to end.
A right or improvement that runs with the land and passes with the deed, such as an easement appurtenant.
Riparian: owners along rivers and streams. Littoral: owners along lakes and oceans.
Water rights go to the first to put water to beneficial use ("first in time, first in right"). Colorado uses this system.
Describes a parcel by distances and directions from a point of beginning; it must return to the POB. Monuments generally control over distances.
Legal description by reference to a recorded subdivision plat.
6 miles × 6 miles = 36 square miles = 36 sections.
1 mile × 1 mile = 1 square mile = 640 acres.
Section 1: northeast corner of the township. Section 36: southeast corner.

cards.front: Acreage of the N 1/2 of the SW 1/4 of a section
Fee simple determinable vs. condition subsequent
cards.back: "So long as" = determinable, reverts automatically (possibility of reverter). "On condition that" = grantor must act (right of reentry).
A life estate measured by the life of someone other than the life tenant.
Remainder: goes to a named third party when a life estate ends. Reversion: goes back to the grantor or grantor's heirs.
Damage or neglect by a life tenant that lowers the property's value for the future owner. It isn't allowed.
Estate for years, periodic tenancy, tenancy at will, tenancy at sufferance.
Ownership by one person or one entity.
Possession, Interest, Time, Title (PITT).

cards.front: Effect of a joint tenant selling their share
cards.back: The buyer becomes a tenant in common; the remaining owners stay joint tenants with each other.

cards.front: Colorado presumption for conveyance to two or more people
cards.back: Tenancy in common, unless the deed expressly declares a joint tenancy (C.R.S. 38-31-101).

cards.front: Does Colorado recognize tenancy by the entirety?
cards.back: No. C.R.S. 38-31-201: an attempted tenancy by the entirety creates a joint tenancy.

cards.front: Is Colorado a community property state?
cards.back: No. Colorado divides marital property by equitable distribution.
Fee title to the unit plus an undivided interest as tenant in common in the common elements.
Shares in a corporation that owns the building plus a proprietary lease; usually treated as personal property.
Property tax and special assessment liens generally come before all other liens, whatever their recording date.
Appurtenant: has dominant and servient parcels and runs with the land. In gross: benefits a person or company and has no dominant parcel.
Merger, release, abandonment, end of necessity or purpose, and (in some states) non-use of a prescriptive easement.

Open, notorious, continuous, exclusive, hostile (adverse) for the statutory period. Colorado: 18 years (C.R.S. 38-41-101), plus clear and convincing proof (cases filed since July 1, 2008) and a good-faith belief of ownership (title vesting since that date).
Government powers: Police power, Eminent domain, Taxation, Escheat.
Public use and just compensation. The legal process is condemnation.
A suit by an owner seeking compensation when government action has effectively taken or damaged the property.
A use that was legal before the current zoning; it's grandfathered but usually can't be expanded or rebuilt after destruction.
Relief from strict zoning requirements (setback, height) because of a hardship unique to the property.
Allows a use the ordinance permits under conditions, such as a church or school in a residential zone.
Rezoning one parcel inconsistently with the comprehensive plan to benefit one owner; often illegal.
Issued after final inspection; allows a building to be legally occupied.
The more restrictive rule generally governs.
Writing, competent grantor, identifiable grantee, consideration recital, granting clause, legal description, grantor's signature, delivery and acceptance.
General: warrants against defects from any time. Special: only defects arising during the grantor's ownership.
No warranties; conveys whatever interest the grantor has, if any. Used to clear clouds on title.
A later buyer wins only if they had no notice AND recorded first. Colorado's statute (C.R.S. 38-35-109) is race-notice.
Survey and inspection matters: encroachments, boundary disputes, parties in possession, unrecorded easements and mechanic's liens.
Owner's: protects the buyer, usually for the price, lasts while the owner or heirs hold an interest. Lender's: protects the lender for the loan amount.

cards.front: Equity of redemption vs. statutory redemption
cards.back: Equity: pay off and stop foreclosure before the sale. Statutory: buy back after the sale, where state law allows.
Testate: dies with a will (devise). Intestate: dies without a will (descent under state statute); no heirs = escheat.

glossary.definition: Land, everything permanently attached to it, and the legal rights of ownership.
Movable property that isn't real property, such as furniture or vehicles. It transfers by bill of sale.
The set of legal rights that come with owning real property: possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, and disposition.
Formerly personal property that has been attached to real estate so that it becomes part of the real property.
Equipment a tenant installs for business use. It remains the tenant's personal property and must be removed by the end of the lease.
Annual crops produced by labor. They're treated as personal property, and a tenant farmer may harvest them after the tenancy ends if the tenant didn't cause it to end.
A right or improvement that belongs to the land and passes with it on transfer, such as an easement appurtenant.
A legal description that traces a parcel's boundaries using distances, directions, and monuments from a point of beginning back to that point.
The fixed starting point of a metes and bounds description, where the description must also end.
A legal description that identifies a parcel by lot and block number on a recorded subdivision plat.
A grid-based legal description system using principal meridians, base lines, townships, and sections. It's used in most western and midwestern states.
In the rectangular survey system, a square 6 miles on a side (36 square miles) divided into 36 sections.
In the rectangular survey system, a 1-mile-square area containing 640 acres. There are 36 in a township.
A unit of land area equal to 43,560 square feet.
An ownership interest of indefinite duration, such as a fee simple or life estate.
A tenant's right to possess property for a period under a lease. It's treated as personal property.
The most complete form of ownership, unlimited in duration and freely transferable or inheritable.
A fee estate that can end if a stated condition occurs or stops, such as a fee simple determinable or a fee simple subject to a condition subsequent.
An estate that lasts for the lifetime of a named person, after which the property passes to a remainderman or reverts to the grantor.
Ownership by a single person or legal entity.
Co-ownership with undivided interests that may be unequal, transferable without consent, and inheritable, with no right of survivorship.
Co-ownership with equal shares and the right of survivorship, traditionally requiring the four unities of possession, interest, time, and title.
The feature of joint tenancy under which a deceased owner's interest passes automatically to the surviving co-owners.
A form of co-ownership for married couples, recognized in some states, with survivorship and protection from one spouse acting alone. Colorado does not recognize it.
A system in some states under which property acquired during marriage is owned equally by both spouses. Colorado is not a community property state.
Ownership of an individual unit in fee simple plus an undivided interest in common elements shared with other owners.
Ownership in which a corporation holds title to a building and residents own shares plus a proprietary lease for their units.
Ownership or use of property divided by recurring time periods, either as a fee interest (timeshare estate) or a contractual right to use.
An arrangement in which a trustor conveys property to a trustee, who holds legal title and manages it for a beneficiary.
Any claim or right held by someone other than the owner that limits the property's use or lowers its value, such as a lien, easement, or restriction.
A creditor's claim against property as security for a debt, which can be enforced by forcing a sale.
A specific, involuntary lien for unpaid contractors, subcontractors, or suppliers who improved the property.
An agreement by which a lien holder accepts a lower priority than another lien.
A non-possessory right to use another person's land for a specific purpose.
An easement that benefits a neighboring (dominant) parcel and burdens the servient parcel. It runs with the land.
An easement that benefits a person or company rather than a neighboring parcel, such as a utility line easement.
An easement acquired by open, continuous, hostile use of another's land for the period set by state law.
Personal, revocable permission to enter another's land for a specific purpose. It isn't an interest in land.
An improvement that extends onto a neighbor's property or into a setback or easement.
Gaining title to another's land by open, notorious, continuous, exclusive, and hostile possession for the statutory period.
Government's authority to regulate property use to protect public health, safety, and welfare. It's the basis of zoning and building codes.
Local laws dividing land into districts and regulating the uses, density, and building dimensions allowed in each.
A use that was lawful before a zoning change but doesn't meet the current ordinance. It may continue, usually with limits.
Permission to depart from the strict requirements of a zoning ordinance because they would cause an unusual hardship.
Permission for a use the zoning ordinance allows only under specified conditions, such as a church in a residential zone.
Local standards for construction, plumbing, electrical, and fire safety, enforced through permits and inspections.
Government's power to take private property for public use with just compensation, through condemnation.
A lawsuit by an owner seeking compensation when government action has effectively taken or damaged the property without formal condemnation.
Transfer of property to the state when an owner dies without a will and without heirs.
A charge against specific properties that benefit from a public improvement. It creates a specific lien.
A private limit on property use written into a deed or recorded declaration.
Covenants, conditions, and restrictions recorded for a subdivision or condominium that bind all owners.
An organization of owners in a planned community or condominium that enforces CC&Rs, maintains common areas, and collects assessments.
A written instrument that conveys title to real property from a grantor to a grantee.
The person who conveys title by deed.
The person who receives title by deed.
A deed in which the grantor warrants title against all defects, including those arising before the grantor owned the property.
A deed in which the grantor warrants title only against defects arising during the grantor's ownership.
A deed that implies the grantor holds title but gives no express warranties against encumbrances.
A deed that conveys whatever interest the grantor has, if any, with no warranties.
A fiduciary deed used by the court-appointed representative of a deceased person's estate to convey estate property.
A formal declaration before a notary or other officer that a signature is genuine and voluntary. Most states require it before a deed can be recorded.
Filing a document affecting real property in the county public records, which gives constructive notice.
Notice the law presumes everyone has, from public records or from inspecting the property.
What a person actually knows, from seeing, hearing, or reading it.
The recorded history of conveyances from the original source of title to the current owner.
A condensed history of all recorded documents affecting a property, usually reviewed by an attorney.
A policy that protects an owner or lender against covered losses from title defects. It's paid for with a one-time premium.
Title free enough from reasonable doubt that a prudent buyer would accept it.
A claim or document that casts doubt on title, such as an unreleased lien or a possible heir's claim.
A lawsuit to establish ownership and remove clouds on title.
Transfer of title without the owner's consent, such as by foreclosure, eminent domain, escheat, or adverse possession.
The legal process by which a lender forces the sale of property to satisfy a defaulted loan.
A borrower's voluntary conveyance of the property to the lender to avoid foreclosure.
A sale for less than the loan balance, in which the lender agrees to accept the net proceeds.
Dying without a valid will. Property then passes to heirs under state succession laws.
The earth's surface, everything below it to the center of the earth, and the airspace above it, including natural things attached to it such as trees and minerals in place.
Land plus everything people have permanently attached to it, such as buildings, fences, and paving.
The rights of owners whose land borders a lake, sea, or ocean to use and enjoy the water and the shoreline.
Trees, perennial shrubs, grass, and other plants that grow without being planted each year. They're treated as part of the real property.
The fixture test that asks how an item is attached to the property (bolted, nailed, plumbed, or wired in) and whether removing it would cause damage.
Acquiring title to property that is added to or left on land you own, such as trade fixtures a tenant leaves behind after the lease ends.
A description of land precise enough to identify exactly one parcel, written using metes and bounds, lot and block, or the rectangular survey system.

A fixed natural or artificial object, such as an iron pin, tree, or road, used to mark a boundary in a metes and bounds description. When a monument and a measured distance conflict, the monument generally controls.
A map of a subdivision, prepared by a surveyor and recorded with the county, that shows each lot and block along with streets and easements.

A main north–south line in the rectangular survey system from which ranges are numbered east and west. Colorado uses the Sixth Principal Meridian, the New Mexico Principal Meridian, and the Ute Meridian.
A main east–west line in the rectangular survey system that crosses a principal meridian; township tiers are numbered north and south of it.
A north–south line in the rectangular survey system drawn every 6 miles east and west of a principal meridian. The columns between them are called ranges.
An east–west line in the rectangular survey system drawn every 6 miles north and south of a base line. The rows between them are called township tiers.
In the rectangular survey system, a square about 24 miles on a side containing 16 townships, bounded by guide meridians and correction lines.
An east–west line (standard parallel) drawn every 24 miles north and south of a base line to adjust the survey grid for the curvature of the earth.
An irregular parcel in the rectangular survey system that can't be a full quarter-quarter section, usually because it lies along a body of water or at the edge of a township.
A reference point or surface, such as mean sea level or a local benchmark, from which surveyors measure elevations and heights.
The degree, quantity, and duration of a person's interest in real property. Estates are either freehold (ownership) or leasehold (tenancy).
The future interest a grantor keeps in a fee simple determinable. If the stated condition is broken, title returns to the grantor automatically.

glossary.term: Fee simple subject to a condition subsequent
glossary.definition: Fee ownership that the grantor can end if a stated condition is broken, using words like "on condition that." The grantor must take action (right of reentry) to get the property back.
The future interest a grantor keeps in a fee simple subject to a condition subsequent. If the condition is broken, the grantor must act to reclaim the property. Also called a power of termination.
A life estate created on purpose by a deed or will, usually lasting for the life tenant's own lifetime.
A life estate measured by the life of someone other than the life tenant, such as "to Ann for the life of Bob."
The future interest a grantor keeps when the property returns to the grantor or the grantor's heirs after a life estate ends.
The third party named to receive the property when a life estate ends.
The future interest held by a remainderman, who takes the property when a life estate ends.
Damage, neglect, or misuse of property by a life tenant or tenant that lowers its value for the future owner.
A life estate created by state law rather than by a deed or will, such as historical dower and curtesy rights of a surviving spouse.
A state-law protection that shields part of the value of a family's home from certain creditors.
A co-owner's share in a whole property, with the right to use all of it, rather than ownership of any particular physical part.
A court action that divides co-owned property among the owners or, if it can't be divided fairly, orders it sold and divides the proceeds.
The four requirements traditionally needed to create a joint tenancy: possession, interest, time, and title. Tenancy in common requires only unity of possession.
In community property states, property a spouse owned before marriage or received by gift or inheritance, which belongs to that spouse alone.
Common elements of a condominium reserved for the use of one or a few units, such as an assigned parking space or a balcony.
The lease a cooperative corporation gives a shareholder, granting the right to occupy a particular unit.
