A timeshare that conveys a fee ownership interest in a property for a recurring period, such as the same week every year.
A timeshare that gives a contractual or lease-type right to use a property for a period, without real property ownership.
The person who creates a trust by conveying property to a trustee. Also called the settlor or grantor.
The person or institution that holds legal title to property in a trust and manages it for the beneficiary.
The person who receives the benefit of property held in a trust.
A legal entity separate from its shareholders that can hold title in severalty. Shareholders have limited liability, but a C corporation's income is taxed twice.
A business in which all partners share management and have unlimited personal liability for the partnership's debts.
A partnership with at least one general partner who manages and has unlimited liability, plus limited partners who are passive investors liable only up to their investment.
A business entity whose members have limited liability and flexible pass-through tax treatment. It's commonly used to hold investment property.
A group of investors pooling money for a real estate investment, usually organized as a partnership or LLC rather than a separate legal form.
Two or more parties joining together for a single project or investment. It isn't a separate legal form and is often organized as a partnership or LLC.

A company that pools investors' money to own or finance real estate and avoids corporate income tax on income it distributes if it meets federal requirements, such as paying out at least 90% of taxable income.
An investment in which the buyer expects a profit from others' management efforts, such as a condo unit that must go into a rental pool. Selling one requires a securities license and registration.
A specific, involuntary lien created by law for unpaid property taxes. It generally takes priority over all other liens.
A general, involuntary lien created when a court judgment against a person is recorded. It attaches to that person's real property in the county.
The order in which liens are paid. The basic rule is first in time, first in right by recording date, except that property tax and special assessment liens generally come first.
Describes a right or restriction that stays attached to the property and binds or benefits later owners when the property is sold.
An easement created on purpose in writing, either granted to someone in a deed or agreement or reserved by a seller when conveying land.
An easement created by law when a parcel is sold without access to a road and the parcels were once under common ownership. It ends when the need ends.
An easement implied from the circumstances and prior use of the land when a parcel is divided.
A wall shared by two adjoining properties along the property line, with each owner holding an easement in the other's half.
The ending of a lesser interest when it and a greater interest come under the same owner, such as an easement ending when one person owns both the dominant and servient parcels.
A written document in which the holder of a right, such as an easement or lien, gives it up.
Giving up a right or use on purpose, shown by conduct and not just by non-use. It can end an easement or a nonconforming use.
Ownership of real property, and the evidence of that ownership.
Adding together the periods of possession of successive adverse possessors who are in privity to reach the required statutory time.
A legal relationship between parties, such as a seller and buyer, that lets one succeed to the other's rights.
A higher standard of proof than "more likely than not," requiring evidence that makes a claim highly probable. Colorado adverse possession claimants must meet it.
A use that benefits the public, such as a road or school. Eminent domain can be used only for a public use.
The payment the government must make when it takes property by eminent domain, usually the property's fair market value.
Compensation for the loss in value of the remaining land when only part of a property is taken by eminent domain.
Latin for "according to value." Ad valorem property taxes are based on a property's value.
A local government's long-range plan for growth and land use, carried out through zoning and other regulations. Also called a master plan.
A state law that gives local governments the authority to enact zoning and other land use regulations.
The minimum distance a building must be from a lot line, street, or other boundary under zoning rules.
A strip of land, such as a park or a light-use district, that separates incompatible uses like homes and heavy industry.
Zoning that allows "higher" uses, such as homes, in a zone set aside for "lower" uses, such as commercial.
Zoning that allows only the use listed for the zone.
Rezoning land to a less intense use, such as from commercial to residential.
Rezoning a single parcel to benefit one owner in a way that conflicts with the comprehensive plan. It's often struck down as illegal.
Changing the zoning of an area through the legislative process. Also called a zoning amendment.
A local board, also called a zoning board of appeals, that hears variance requests and appeals of zoning decisions.
Permission from the local building department to construct or alter a building, which lets the department enforce building codes through inspections.
A document the building department issues after a building passes final inspection, allowing people to legally occupy it.
A charge on developers to help pay for public facilities, such as schools, parks, and roads, that new development requires.

glossary.term: Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act
glossary.definition: A federal law requiring developers who sell or lease certain unimproved lots through interstate commerce to register and give buyers a property report. Subdivisions under 25 lots are exempt.
The disclosure document a developer must give lot buyers under the Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act before they sign. Buyers can generally revoke within 7 days.
A promise in a deed or recorded declaration about how property will or won't be used. A breach is usually remedied by an injunction or damages.
A deed restriction that, if broken, may let the grantor reclaim title. Courts prefer to treat restrictions as covenants to avoid this forfeiture.
A court order requiring a person to do or stop doing something, such as removing an encroachment or obeying a deed restriction.
A doctrine that lets a court refuse to enforce a right when the person waited unreasonably long to assert it.
Any transfer of title to property, whether voluntary (deed or will) or involuntary.
The passing of a deceased person's property to heirs under state law when there is no valid will.
A written document directing how a person's property passes at death.
The slow addition of land by water depositing soil along a shore or riverbank. The added land belongs to the owner of the land it attaches to.
The gradual wearing away of land by water, wind, or other natural forces, which reduces the owner's land.
The part of a deed with words of conveyance, such as "grants" or "conveys," showing the grantor's intent to transfer title.
The final steps that make a deed transfer title: the grantor delivers it and the grantee accepts it during the grantor's lifetime.
The "to have and to hold" clause of a deed, which defines the estate being granted.
The deed covenant that the grantor owns the property and has the right to convey it.
The deed covenant that the property has no encumbrances except those listed in the deed.
The deed covenant that the grantor will sign any additional documents needed to perfect the grantee's title.
The deed covenant that the grantor will defend the title against all lawful claims.
A deed from a trustee conveying property held in a trust or sold at a deed-of-trust foreclosure. It generally carries only limited warranties.
A deed given to the buyer at a court-ordered sale, such as a judicial foreclosure. It carries no warranties.
A fiduciary deed from a court-appointed guardian conveying a ward's property, usually with limited warranties.
A fiduciary deed from a court-appointed conservator conveying a protected person's property, usually with limited warranties.
A recording statute under which the first buyer to record wins, regardless of notice.
A recording statute under which a later buyer without notice of an earlier unrecorded deed wins.
A missing link in the chain of title, where the records don't show how title passed from one owner to the next.
An attorney's written opinion, based on reviewing an abstract or the public records, about who holds title and what defects exist.
A title insurer's promise, issued before closing, to issue a policy once listed requirements are met, showing the exceptions the policy won't cover.
Title insurance that covers defects in the public records plus certain hidden risks like forgery, but excludes matters only a survey or inspection would reveal.
Title insurance that removes some or all standard exceptions, such as survey matters and parties in possession, usually after a survey and inspection.
The event at which the buyer pays, the seller delivers the deed, liens are paid off, the new loan is funded, and documents are recorded. Also called settlement.
Foreclosure in which the lender sues and a court orders the property sold, often by a sheriff.
Foreclosure without a lawsuit, under a power of sale in the deed of trust. Colorado uses a public trustee for most of these.
A clause in a deed of trust or mortgage that allows the property to be sold without a court action if the borrower defaults.
A borrower's right to stop a foreclosure by paying off the debt before the sale.
A right some states give to buy back the property after a foreclosure sale within a set period.
A personal judgment against a borrower for the amount still owed when a foreclosure sale brings less than the debt, where state law allows it.
A person who makes a will.
A gift of real property by will.
The person who receives real property by will.
A written amendment to a will.
The court-supervised process of proving a will, paying the deceased person's debts, and distributing the property.
